sources.title: OpenJDK 21u AbstractQueuedSynchronizer source at fixed revision 7da13d210d4c6024083c57f0b8432fc6fee19a90

claims.text: Java 21 defines AQS as a framework for blocking locks and related synchronizers based on an internal FIFO wait queue and one atomically updated int synchronization state whose meaning is defined by subclasses.

Subclasses implement protected tryAcquire/tryRelease and/or shared counterparts while AQS final public methods perform the queuing and blocking mechanics; the protected methods should be thread-safe, short and normally non-blocking.

For Java 21 exclusive acquisition, AQS invokes tryAcquire at least once, then queues and may repeatedly block/unblock and retry until successful; release invokes tryRelease and, when release permits progress, unblocks a queued thread. Shared mode uses the same FIFO queue and may cascade signals.

The FIFO queue does not automatically enforce FIFO acquisition because acquisition checks occur before enqueueing and new threads may barge; hasQueuedPredecessors can be used by fair synchronizers, while the Java 21 API states that default barging generally offers higher throughput and scalability.
Java 21 ConditionObject support releases the saved synchronization state while waiting and eventually reacquires the saved state before returning; a condition signal does not directly grant the lock.

Internal node layout, links, parking and cancellation cleanup are implementation details rather than the public AQS contract; this candidate binds such source-level discussion to OpenJDK 21u revision 7da13d210d4c6024083c57f0b8432fc6fee19a90.
